title: Czech inflation undershoots while the forecast points to firmer short rates
summary: The Czech National Bank’s 6 February explanation of its winter forecast brings together two outcomes that normally pull a rates view in opposite directions. The Bank Board held its two-week repo rate at 3.5% and judged inflation risks balanced. The forecast lowered average 2026 headline inflation to 1.6%, yet raised its 2026 GDP growth and average three-month PRIBOR projections. Author Zdeněk Pikhart explains that a temporary reduction in measured energy costs leads the near-term inflation decline. The persistence of wage and housing pressures, together with demand projected to exceed the economy’s potential, matters more for inflation at the policy horizon. The forecast is consistent with broadly stable short rates in the first half of 2026 and a subsequent modest rise. That model-consistent path is distinct from the Board’s actual February decision.

Headline inflation had slowed to 2.1% at the end of 2025. An earlier koruna appreciation reduced fuel costs and slowed price growth for food and beverages. Favourable oil and agricultural commodity prices were expected to support that pattern in 2026. The main further downward step early in the year came from transferring the supported energy sources fee to the state budget. The household price index can fall relative to its prior path as the payer changes without requiring a comparable weakening in underlying spending. Once the year-on-year comparison no longer includes that transfer, inflation is expected to rise modestly again. The chart shows the central path running below the 2% target through 2026 and close to it in the marked 2027 policy horizon. Its bands widen as the horizon extends. Neither the bands nor the table warrant interpreting any single forecast print as certain (inflation discussion and fan chart).

The domestic price evidence goes in the other direction. Core inflation was just below 3%, supported by services prices. Wage growth remained brisk in a tight labour market. Imputed rent also contributed, reflecting the rising prices of new residential properties amid stronger household income and lending. This matters for interpreting monetary transmission: a stronger currency can alleviate traded-goods inflation at the same time that credit and incomes sustain prices in the housing-related part of the domestic basket. The table raises average nominal wage growth for 2026 by 0.4 percentage points to 6.1%; the 2027 forecast is 5.0%. The projection therefore incorporates a slowdown without assuming that the labour-cost channel disappears.

The article attributes most of the near-term growth impetus to consumption, with real wage growth and fiscal easing supporting households while their saving rate stays near current levels. Investment is expected to change composition. Public fixed investment, supported by EU funds, leads initially; private investment becomes the larger contributor in the second half as the external economy recovers. German fiscal expansion is expected to support foreign demand for Czech exports. Yet stronger export production and investment also generate imports. Net trade is projected to make a broadly neutral contribution to GDP in both years, despite robust export performance. This is why rising gross exports alone would be a poor test of the 2.9% growth forecast for each year (activity discussion and forecast table).

The revisions make the policy arithmetic clearer. Compared with the previous forecast, projected inflation is 0.6 percentage points lower in 2026 and 0.4 points lower in 2027, at 1.6% and 2.1%. GDP growth is 0.5 and 0.1 points higher, respectively. The three-month PRIBOR projections are annual averages of 3.6% and 4.0%, up 0.1 and 0.2 points; these numbers are neither the repo rate nor year-end policy targets. The koruna had traded near CZK 24.3 per euro since the start of 2026. Faster cost growth at home than abroad implies a small depreciation in the forecast and a subsequent level near 24.5 per euro. As the disinflationary effect of earlier appreciation fades, higher import prices, wages and property prices put pressure on inflation at the horizon (exchange-rate discussion and table).

The Board lists faster money growth through lending to households and government, additional public spending, wage pressure and persistent service inflation as upside risks. A stronger koruna, trade barriers that weaken global activity, underperformance in parts of the euro area, or a global asset-price correction in highly indebted economies could pull in the opposite direction. The article mentions industrial restructuring and potential productivity gains from AI as longer-term issues and supplies no quantified AI gain for this forecast. For a rates investor the discriminating test is whether weakness spreads beyond administered energy and currency-sensitive prices into domestic demand and services. The release gives no contemporaneous investor consensus against which to call this forecast a positive or negative surprise.

questions.question: How much of the projected undershoot survives removal of the change in energy financing?
questions.detail: The article identifies a change in the payer of the energy fee as the main early-year driver but does not give a full underlying inflation path stripped of that effect. Compare the CNB’s decomposition, official CPI expenditure weights and market-services prices across successive releases. This matters for short-end rates because a mechanical reversal can bring headline inflation back to target without signalling extra pressure from demand.

questions.question: Are real wages supporting spending or replenishing saving?
questions.detail: The consumption projection assumes strong real income gains and a broadly stable saving rate. A rise in precautionary saving would weaken the projected positive output gap even if wage growth matched the forecast. Examine official household accounts, retail volumes and labour income together, alongside the central bank’s cyclical indicators. The mix helps assess whether tighter short rates later in the horizon would still be consistent with the forecast.

questions.question: Would an export rebound change net demand for koruna or mainly raise imports?
questions.detail: Germany’s expected fiscal expansion supports orders, yet the model has net trade contributing roughly zero to GDP. The split between imported inputs, domestic value added and the timing of capital-goods imports matters for currency exposure. Use official trade-volume and investment breakdowns and the central bank’s external forecast. Assess separately whether the koruna is moving because of trade volumes or because domestic costs and financial conditions have changed.
